A content delivery network solves a simple problem: a website's main storage, called an origin server, might sit in one city, while people trying to view that site are scattered across the world. The farther the request has to travel, the slower the page feels. So the network places copies of the site's content at many edge locations — smaller storage points positioned close to different regions. When someone requests a page and the nearby edge location already has a saved copy ready to serve, that's called a cache hit, and the content arrives almost instantly without needing to contact the distant origin server at all.

Think of it like a chain of neighborhood libraries stocking popular books close to home instead of everyone traveling to one central archive across the country. Most people find what they need nearby, and only rare or updated requests get sent back to the archive. This setup reduces waiting time, spreads out demand so no single location gets overwhelmed, and keeps things working smoothly even during traffic spikes, since load is shared across many points rather than piled onto one.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|------|---------------|-----------------|
| Origin server | The original, central storage holding a website's true content | It's the source everything else copies from |
| Edge location | A nearby storage point that keeps copies of content | It shortens the distance content has to travel |
| Cache hit | When requested content is already saved nearby | It means faster loading with less waiting |
| Latency | The delay between asking for content and receiving it | Lower delay makes browsing feel smooth and responsive |
